question: A Canadian household includes a 27-year-old adult, their mother and their grandmother, all living together. Why is this classified as multigenerational rather than just a parent living with an adult child in Statistics Canada's 2021 Census studies?
generated_answer:
According to Statistics Canada's 2021 Census studies, a household is considered multigenerational if it includes at least three generations of a family. In this case, the household consists of a 27-year-old adult (first generation), their mother (second generation), and their grandmother (third generation). The presence of three generations living together meets the criteria for a multigenerational household.

If only the 27-year-old adult and their mother were living together, it would be considered a parent living with an adult child, but not multigenerational. The addition of the grandmother, representing a third generation, is what classifies this household as multigenerational.

Statistics Canada uses this definition to capture the complexity of family relationships and living arrangements in Canadian households, and to provide insights into the changing demographics and social structures of the country.
